summary: This guide describes how schools in the district have started student-led recycling programs since September 14th, 2023, and lays out steps for replicating them. The steps include winning administration buy-in, running a waste audit, forming a Green Team, educating students, setting up stations, integrating recycling into the curriculum, partnering with recycling facilities, and running challenges. Each step is illustrated with a named teacher, student or coordinator at a particular school, and the guide ends with measuring and celebrating results.
one_line: A step-by-step guide, with examples from district schools, to launching student-led recycling programs that began in September 2023.
key_facts: Student-led recycling initiatives began on September 14th, 2023, at schools such as Lincoln Elementary and Franklin High School.
Laura Stevens, a teacher at Roosevelt Middle School, calls recycling "an educational tool that helps students learn about their impact on the planet."

George Martinez, Principal of Kennedy High School, has advocated for sustainability since November 2023 and suggests presenting facts that recycling reduces landfill waste, saves energy and may save the school money.
Kimberly Cho, an environmental science teacher, led a waste audit at Jefferson Elementary on October 5th, 2023, in which students sorted trash to find recyclable materials.
Oliver King, a senior at Adams High School, formed a Green Team with peers in early September 2023; it meets weekly to plan, coordinate and promote recycling.
Jessica Li of the Green Team at Washington Junior High saw a spike in participation after posters, classroom presentations and a recycling-themed assembly.
On December 1st, 2023, sustainability coordinator Emily Johnson helped launch recycling stations at Madison Middle School, with bins in every classroom, the cafeteria and common areas, plus signage.
Since January 2024, Andrew Smith, a science teacher at Monroe High School, has incorporated lessons on waste and recycling into his classes.

In February 2024, parent volunteer Susan Anderson coordinated with a nearby recycling facility to pick up and handle Lincoln Elementary's recyclables; the facility also provided data on the amount recycled.
Thomas Lee, student council president at Roosevelt Middle School, described a month-long recycling challenge in March 2024 in which homerooms competed and the winning class got a prize.
By April 2024, several schools such as Hamilton Elementary reported a significant reduction in waste output.
Earth Day celebrations are cited as good platforms for acknowledging students' work on recycling.
